title: Mindfulness-based Psychoeducation, Burnout, and Cognitive Appraisal in University Students: The Negative Role of Burnout in Predicting Later Mindful Attention
abstract: This study examined the associations among participation in a mindfulness-based psychoeducational program, academic burnout, cognitive appraisal, mindful attention, and affect in university students. Using a quasi-experimental, three-wave longitudinal design, 166 students participated in either a mindfulness-based program (n = 64) or a control condition (n = 102). Participants completed measures of burnout, mindful attention, cognitive appraisals, and affect at baseline, midpoint, and post-program. Longitudinal associations were analyzed using cross-lagged panel modeling and mediation analyses within a structural equation modeling framework. Participation in the program was associated with higher mindful attention at post-program. Core burnout emerged as a key mechanism, partially mediating the association between program participation and mindful attention over time. Program participation was modeled as a dichotomous indicator of group membership (0 = control, 1 = program). Although no direct association between program participation and burnout was observed at post-program, significant indirect pathways indicated that lower burnout was associated with subsequent improvements in mindful attention and self-concept of own abilities. In addition, the self-concept of own abilities functioned as a mediator between group membership and later burnout, highlighting the role of secondary cognitive appraisals as personal resources. The findings suggest that mindfulness-based psychoeducational programs in academic settings may support appraisal-related processes and mindful attention, thereby supporting student well-being.
